content: Hives, which are raised bumps on the skin, can occur as a reaction to certain medications. Other symptoms that may arise include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting, stomach cramps, and joint pain. Dicloxacillin, like many antibiotics, can lead to an overgrowth of bacteria called Clostridioides difficile (commonly referred to as C. diff) in the gut, which may result in antibiotic-associated diarrhea. This condition can develop even up to two months after stopping the medication. If you experience watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in your stool, severe stomach cramps, or fever after starting or finishing dicloxacillin, contact your healthcare provider immediately. Seizures have been reported in some individuals taking dicloxacillin. Seizures can present in various forms, some of which may not be easily recognizable. If you notice muscle twitching, jerking, spasms, tremors, stiffening of the arms or legs, feelings of anxiety, confusion, dizziness, lightheadedness, or loss of consciousness, stop taking dicloxacillin and seek medical attention promptly. Kidney damage is another potential side effect of dicloxacillin. If you experience any of these symptoms, contact your healthcare provider immediately. Dicloxacillin can also cause blood disorders, such as eosinophilia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, neutropenia, leukopenia, or bone marrow depression. Symptoms of blood disorders include fever, shortness of breath, pale or yellowish skin, easy bruising or bleeding, frequent infections, unusual weakness or tiredness, dizziness, lightheadedness, headaches, or an abnormal or rapid heartbeat. If you suspect a blood disorder, stop taking dicloxacillin and seek medical help immediately. Liver damage, also known as hepatotoxicity, is another serious side effect of dicloxacillin. Symptoms of liver damage include nausea, vomiting, stomach or abdominal pain, fever, weakness, unusual tiredness, itching, loss of appetite, light-colored stools, dark-colored urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). If you experience any of these symptoms, contact your healthcare provider right away. Certain individuals should not take dicloxacillin, particularly those with known allergies to dicloxacillin or any of its ingredients. Your pharmacist can provide a complete list of ingredients in the specific product you are prescribed. Additionally, dicloxacillin should only be taken as prescribed by a healthcare provider. It is important to take the medication on an empty stomach with a large glass of water (at least 4 ounces or 120 milliliters) at least one hour before or two hours after a meal. Avoid lying down or taking the medication right before bed. Do not share dicloxacillin with others, even if they have similar symptoms, as it may harm them. Before starting dicloxacillin, inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions and any medications, vitamins, or supplements you are taking. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medications, as well as herbal products. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, discuss this with your healthcare provider, as dicloxacillin passes into breast milk and its effects on pregnancy are not fully known. Dicloxacillin is best absorbed on an empty stomach. While it is unclear if alcohol directly interacts with dicloxacillin, heavy alcohol consumption can weaken the immune system and impair the body’s ability to fight infections. Always inform your healthcare provider about any other medications or supplements you are taking, as dicloxacillin may interact with certain drugs, such as tetracyclines, probenecid (commonly used for gout), or warfarin (a blood thinner). Avoid taking additional medications, including over-the-counter drugs like antacids or laxatives, without consulting your physician. If you accidentally take too much dicloxacillin, seek medical help immediately by calling 911 or contacting a poison control center at 800-222-1222. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take double or extra doses. It is crucial to complete the full prescribed course of dicloxacillin, even if your symptoms improve, to reduce the risk of developing antibiotic-resistant infections in the future. The most common side effects of dicloxacillin include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and a black hairy tongue. If these side effects bother you, inform your healthcare provider. Serious side effects, while less common, require immediate medical attention. These include severe allergic reactions (e.g., breathing difficulties, swelling of the face or throat, hives, or a racing heart), antibiotic-associated diarrhea, seizures, kidney damage, blood disorders, or liver damage. Always report any suspected side effects to your healthcare provider or the FDA’s MedWatch program at 800-FDA-1088.
